sources.claim: NIST PQC FAQ: Grover's algorithm 'will provide little or no advantage in attacking AES, and AES 128 will remain secure for decades to come'; machines 'may be years or decades away but could eventually break many of today's widely used cryptographic systems'
NIST, Aug 13, 2024: NIST releases first 3 finalized post-quantum encryption standards: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)

Help Net Security, Oct 28, 2026: a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could break some widely used methods; NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use after 2035; attackers could collect encrypted data and hold it until quantum technology allows them to read it, 'harvest now, decrypt later'
Quantum Computing Report on final NIST IR 8547: RSA, DH/ECDH, ECDSA, EdDSA listed as quantum-vulnerable; deprecated after 2030, completely disallowed after 2035; AES-128/192/256 remain approved

post.instagram_caption:
"Quantum computers will break all encryption." Not quite.

Encryption comes in two main kinds. Public-key encryption, like RSA, is the kind a big enough quantum computer could break. The other kind, like AES, scrambles the data itself, and NIST says AES-128 will remain secure for decades to come. NIST also says machines able to break today's public-key systems may be years or decades away.

The risk is still real: attackers could collect encrypted data now and read it later, known as "harvest now, decrypt later". That is why NIST released its first 3 quantum-safe standards in August 2024, and its final timeline deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallows it after 2035 (Help Net Security).

The lesson: it is not doomsday, it is a deadline.

Source: NIST, Post-Quantum Cryptography FAQ and Aug 13, 2024 release; Help Net Security, Oct 28, 2026.

post.youtube_description:
The claim: quantum computers will break all encryption. The reality: a big enough quantum computer could break public-key encryption like RSA, but NIST says AES-128 will remain secure for decades. The risk is real because attackers could harvest encrypted data now and decrypt it later, so NIST released its first 3 post-quantum standards in August 2024 and plans to deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow it after 2035.
